newsitem.title: USA: Stocks fall on rate fears, tobacco ruling.
newsitem.headline: Stocks fall on rate fears, tobacco ruling.

text.p: Stocks fell on Friday as investors put quarterly earnings behind them and worried about interest rates, high technology shares and a new ruling on tobacco regulation.
At 1 p.m. EDT, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 48.96 points, or 0.72 percent, at 6.743.29, after falling more than 60 points earlier.
In the broader market, declines led advancing issues by 15 to six on volume of about 227 million shares on the NYSE.
The technology-laden Nasdaq Composite index was down 11.34 points, or 0.92 percent, at 1,216.76.

"A real fear that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in May has pervaded the market and erased the gains it had been making in several areas, particularly techs and transports," said Peggy Farley, chief executive at Amas Securities.

But a rate hike is not a foregone conclusion, she said. "There is a lot of ammunition to support the argument that inflation has been contained, wages are not surging higher and that the economy is slowing down."
Bonds edged lower, with the 30-year Treasury down 3/32, raising its yield to 7.14 percent from Thursday's close of 7.13 percent. The price and yield move in opposite directions.
The Dow also sagged due to sell-offs in components International Business Machines Corp., down 2-3/8 at 151-3/8, and Philip Morris Cos. Inc., off 2-1/2 at 39-1/8.
Investors took profits on IBM a day after Big Blue's stock soared on surprisingly strong first-quarter earnings.
"IBM is an example of a stock that gets jerked around too much by Wall Street's flight of fancy," said Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford Brown & Catherwood.
"The action in the markets that we have seen recently is more suggestive of a gambling casino than a rational investment process. You can't look at it on a daily basis and make much sense of it."

Philip Morris took a beating along with other tobacco stocks after U.S. District Court Judge William Osteen in Greensboro, N.C., ruled that the Food and Drug Administration can regulate the sales and labeling of cigarettes.
However, he ruled that the FDA cannot make regulations on promotion and advertising of tobacco products.
While the ruling was mixed, Farley said Wall Street hates regulations on industries to begin with, and that this one adds to the other risks facing investors in the tobacco companies.
